# Sandbox Creation

This package owns UI-independent client-side preparation and submission of
sandbox create requests.

- Frontends provide typed options; this package resolves source refs, snapshots
  dirty local workspaces, captures local user identity, captures the local Git
  authorship, derives the origin keys `discobox ls` filters on (`OriginKeys`,
  over the root a create records for its source, `SourceRoot`), classifies
  environment and secret inputs, parses `--grant` (`ParseGrants`), builds the API body, and submits prompt sandbox
  creates.
- Every path placed in the sandbox is judged by the sandbox's platform
  (`PromptOptions.Platform`, through `sandboxpath`; ADR 0145 §6), never by this
  machine's: where a source lands and the working root it lands under. This
  machine's account is sent only to a sandbox with POSIX ids (Linux); any other
  has one account its template provisions and refuses a user naming ids, groups
  or a home (ADR 0145 §5), so it is sent none. The frontend supplies the platform,
  read from the pool the create lands on — `--pool`'s, which the create then
  asks for (`PromptOptions.PoolID`), or the project's default pool, which is
  where the server puts a create that names none (`App.newSandboxPlacement`). A
  pool that has declared no platform is taken as Linux, which every pool from
  before platforms is, and so is the default pool of a caller the server
  refuses those reads (a discobox creating another); such a caller naming
  `--pool` is refused, because the platform it chose is one it cannot learn.
- Git authorship is read with git's own resolution from the source directory, so
  a repository-local `user.email` beats the global one. Unset stays unset: git is
  the authority on whether an identity is configured, and a `$USER@$(hostname)`
  fallback here would only relocate the wrong answer
  ([ADR 0042](../../../docs/adr/0042-git-authorship-identity-is-a-first-class-sandbox-property.md)).
  This inference belongs to the prompt path only — `discobox admin box create` is
  flag-driven and reads nothing from the environment.
- Local user identity is captured from the client machine, except on Windows,
  which has no POSIX identity to capture and instead sends a fixed one: `discobox`,
  uid/gid 1000, home left to the sandbox. Translating a SID and a `C:\Users`
  home yields nothing usable, and sending nothing means the image's own user
  ([ADR 0025](../../../docs/adr/0025-the-sandbox-user-is-one-contract-resolved-inside-the-sandbox.md)
  §5) — root on most harness images. A stated identity is not a guess about the
  local machine, because there is no local answer to get wrong.
- Every identity sent carries both ids, because sandbox create refuses an account
  named without its uid and an id outside root and 1000–60000
  ([ADR 0141](../../../docs/adr/0141-a-sandbox-account-is-created-with-an-id-the-guest-gives-accounts.md)).
  An id the host has that the guest cannot give an account is replaced here, not
  dropped: a uid outside the range (a macOS account's 501) becomes 1000, a gid
  outside it (macOS's 20, Linux's `users` 100) becomes the uid, and a name no
  Linux account can have becomes `discobox`. The server refuses rather than
  clamps, so this is the one place the choice is made. A root host asks for
  nobody.
- A local source keeps its own absolute path inside a **Linux** sandbox **when
  that path is one a sandbox may hold** — a child of `/home`, `/Users`, `/mnt`,
  `/workspace`, `/Volumes`, `/media`, `/srv`, `/opt`, `/data` or `/var/home`
  (the real home path on an ostree system, where `/home` is a symlink)
  (`mirrorableSourceRoots`), minus the paths the image itself occupies
  (`sandboxOwnedPaths`, which is `/opt/discobox`) — so a path means the same
  thing on both sides of the boundary. Anywhere else it is placed
  where a source with no host path goes: the primary at `/workspace/source`, a
  reference at `/workspace/<name>` (a declared one at the sibling path its
  checkout would have had), with the requested subdirectory honored by
  its position within the repository. The destination is a mount target — the
  sandbox-agent binds `/.discobox/sources/<slug>` onto it — and the sandbox is a
  systemd machine that owns some of those directories: a source targeted at
  `/tmp` is mounted onto a tmpfs systemd puts there during boot, so the discobox
  comes up healthy with nothing in it. It is a placement rule and not a refusal,
  because the host directory is the caller's and the mount point is ours; see
  [ADR 26-09-09-044](../../../docs/adr/26-09-09-044-a-source-keeps-its-host-path-only-where-a-sandbox-may-hold-it.md).
  The roots are not a guarantee: a repository rooted exactly at the sandbox
  user's home (`/home/<name>`) is mirrored over it and the harness volumes
  under it, a known collision the client cannot see because it does not know
  which user the image resolves to (ADR 26-09-09-044 §1).
  On Windows it keeps that path in
  the spelling WSL gives it: `E:\src\project` becomes `/mnt/e/src/project`, the
  drive letter lowercased because that is how `/mnt` is spelled and the rest left
  in the case it has on the host. A Windows path cannot be mirrored verbatim —
  the sandbox runs Linux, and the daemon rejects `E:\src\project` as not
  absolute — but it already has a POSIX name, so the mapping stays one-to-one
  instead of collapsing every source onto one container directory. A path with no
  drive letter has no `/mnt` name — a UNC share, or a path already inside a
  distro — and falls back the same way an unmirrorable POSIX path does. One
  predicate answers both (`sandboxSourceRoot`), and one routine places the
  result (`placeRunSource`). A sandbox of any other platform keeps no host
  path: it is a VM that shares no filesystem with this machine (ADR 0126), and
  the roots above are a Linux container's, so every source in it is placed by
  name under its working root (`C:\workspace\source` on Windows).
- A source's path on this machine and its path in the sandbox are therefore two
  different things off a POSIX host, and the code that reads the client's disk —
  `.discobox/sources.json`, the checkout beside the primary source — takes the
  first, while destinations and reference keys take the second.

- A GitHub repository may be named short — `owner/repo` or
  `github.com/owner/repo`, with or without `@REF` — and is expanded to
  `https://github.com/owner/repo.git` (`ExpandGitHubShorthand`) only when no
  such path exists locally: both spellings are valid relative paths, and a
  directory that is there always wins. The CLI expands `-C` once, at flag
  validation, and the console expands a source typed by hand the same way.

- Whether a dirty workspace is snapshotted is the caller's policy
  (`PromptOptions.IncludeDirty`), and asking is the caller's UI
  (`ConfirmIncludeDirty`); this package decides only when the question applies.
  See the CLI design doc's "Uncommitted Work at Create".
- A source directory in no repository asks the same question about the whole
  directory (`ConfirmCopyDirectory`), answered by the same `IncludeDirty`
  policy, and this package measures what would be copied for the frontend to
  show while it asks (`MeasureDirectory`, polled through `DirectoryWalk.Total`).
  Both frontends count the same thing the same way; only where the number is
  drawn is theirs.
- Resolution can answer "no source": declining that question returns the zero
  `resolvedRunSource` (`resolved()` reports it), and the request is built with no
  `config.source` exactly as `NoSource` builds it. A reference that answers the
  same way is dropped instead
  ([ADR 0077](../../../docs/adr/0077-declining-a-directory-copy-creates-a-discobox-with-no-source.md)).
  An empty directory is a different case — it is not asked about and becomes an
  empty source, placed by the same rule as any other local one.
- `PromptOptions.NoSource` builds a request with no `config.source` at all —
  the shape the harness configure sandbox already had, reached deliberately.
  `Source` is then only what the origin and the Git authorship are read from, so
  a sourceless sandbox is still one you started here and listed here. A ref is
  refused rather than dropped, since there is nothing to check it out of; extra
  sources are unaffected, and declared ones fall away with the checkout that
  would have declared them. See the CLI design doc's "No Source At All".
- `PromptOptions.Include` names extra sources, resolved exactly as the primary
  source is and filed as the request's `sourceCodeReferences` under the sandbox
  directory each lands in. This package settles their slugs and destinations;
  see the CLI design doc's "Extra Sources".
- The primary source's own `.discobox/sources.json` names more of them
  (`declared.go`). It is read here, on the client, because deciding what a
  declared source resolves to means looking at this machine's disk for a
  checkout of it — which is also why it is not a field of `.discobox/project.json`,
  read by pool-agent out of the materialized clone. Reporting is the frontend's
  (`ReportDeclaredSource`); this package prints nothing. See the CLI design
  doc's "Declared Sources" and
  [ADR 0056](../../../docs/adr/0056-a-repository-declares-the-sources-it-is-worked-on-with.md).
- `DeliverSource` pushes the sources the server marked push-delivered — the
  server decides that per source — out of the `LocalSources` the create
  returned, records each delivered commit as the origin lease ref a later
  `discobox push` leases against
  ([ADR 0058](../../../docs/adr/0058-a-push-delivered-source-has-a-pool-side-origin.md)
  §6), and reports completion only once every push has landed, since that
  report resumes the sandbox. It is a no-op when nothing awaits a push, so
  callers invoke it unconditionally. See the CLI design doc's "Origin and
  Source Delivery".
- Delivery is also reachable from outside a create: `PendingSourcePushes`,
  `NewLocalSources`, and `CheckDeliverable` let `discobox push` hand a discobox
  parked in `awaiting_source` the source its create never delivered, out of the
  repositories still on the client. The push and the completion call are the
  same `DeliverSource`; only where the repositories come from differs — a create
  has just resolved them, a later delivery finds them again from each source's
  recorded local directory. See the CLI design doc's "Re-delivering Source".
- A source directory in no Git repository gets a throwaway repository built over
  it — after the user has been asked whether to copy it at all — and is
  delivered by push. Create returns every source's repository as
  `LocalSources`, which delivery pushes out of and the caller closes; see the
  CLI design doc's "A Directory That Is Not a Repository" and
  [ADR 0045](../../../docs/adr/0045-a-directory-with-no-repository-is-delivered-by-push.md).
- A source repository with no commits — an unborn HEAD, which is what `git init`
  leaves — is resolved into the same shape without building anything: the empty
  base commit, the snapshot, and their refs go into the user's own repository,
  no branch moves, and the source records `noLocalCommits` rather than
  `noLocalRepository`, so it is pushed but stays deliverable afterwards. Nobody
  is asked. The two questions about an unborn repository — is HEAD one, and
  what does the working tree hold with no HEAD to read it against — come from
  `internal/gitunborn`, because `discobox apply` asks them again coming back
  ([ADR 0084](../../../docs/adr/0084-the-first-apply-into-a-repository-with-no-commits-is-its-history.md)).
  See the CLI design doc's "A Repository With No Commits" and
  [ADR 0083](../../../docs/adr/0083-a-repository-with-no-commits-is-uncommitted-work-on-an-empty-base.md).
- A source repository whose `.git` is not a real directory — a linked worktree
  or submodule checkout — records `noLocalGitDirectory`, so it is pushed rather
  than bound: a bound origin is only ever the repository's own Git directory.
  See the CLI design doc's "A Repository Whose `.git` Is Not Its Git Directory"
  and [ADR 0093](../../../docs/adr/0093-a-local-sources-origin-is-its-git-directory.md).
- A local source checked out at a branch records the URL of the remote that
  branch tracks (`upstreamUrl`, `localUpstreamURL`), which the sandbox adds as
  its `upstream` remote — its `origin` is this repository, so the project's real
  remote is otherwise unknown there. It is the remote's first URL, the one Git
  fetches from: as written when written in full, so this machine's `insteadOf`
  rewrites (https to ssh for a key the sandbox lacks) stay here, and as Git
  resolves it otherwise, so an alias like `gh:org/repo` arrives as a real URL.
  Credentials written into it are dropped, and a remote the sandbox cannot
  reach (another local branch, a path on this machine) sends nothing rather
  than a broken remote.
- Do not depend on `internal/cli` or `internal/tui`. Both frontends consume this
  package through their adapters.
- Keep terminal waiting, attach, and rendering in the frontend packages; those
  behaviors begin after sandbox creation. The one thing that does not begin
  after it is naming the steps taken here: `CreatePromptSandbox` and
  `DeliverSource` take a `Report` and call it as they enter each one, because
  no round trip can tell a process what it is currently doing
  ([ADR 0060](../../../docs/adr/0060-provisioning-progress-is-a-recorded-phase-the-client-polls.md)).
  The words are `Step` constants here so the two frontends cannot describe one
  stage differently; where the line is drawn and when it is cleared is theirs.
- Not every line is a step this client takes. `ProvisionStatus` renders what the
  pool agent recorded on the discobox — a phase, and for a pull its byte and
  layer counts — ignoring a phase older than `ProvisionProgressFresh`. `Status`
  is the entry point every narrated wait uses: when the sandbox's answer is only
  `StepWaitingForPool`, it reads the pool (`PoolReader`) and renders what the
  pool's driver recorded instead (`PoolProvisionStatus`). `awaitSourceRequested`
  reports it through the same `Report` as it waits, out of the reads that wait is
  making anyway. It lives here rather than in a frontend for the same reason the
  `Step` constants do, and because `internal/cli`'s other narrated waits — the
  attach watch and the wait for a provisioned sandbox — render from it too.
  A discobox with nothing left to provision renders nothing, which leaves the
  caller's own step standing rather than blanking it.

# Proxy Design

## Package Role

`proxy` is the reusable pool-scoped network proxy component.
`pool-agent/proxyagent` runs it and uses its certificate preparation output when
launching sandboxes, but the proxy package owns certificates, traffic policy,
HTTP/SOCKS handling, sentinel secret swapping, disk response caching, and audit
persistence.

The component lives in the root module so pool-agent and sandbox-agent share its
configuration and certificate material contracts without depending on server
internals. It has no logger of its own: the datapath, cache, audit writer, and
retention sweep report through OpenTelemetry spans (`proxy.*`).

## Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
```

The pool proxy requires client certificates. Client identity is the verified
mTLS certificate's CommonName (the sandbox ID; the serial when the CN is empty)
and is attached to every HTTP audit row, SOCKS connect row, header injection
decision, destination policy decision, cache event, and upgraded-stream audit
row. The listener sniffs each connection's first byte: `0x05` is served as
SOCKS5, an ASCII capital letter as HTTP, and anything else (SOCKS4 included) is
closed. Every allowed `CONNECT` is MITM'd with a per-host certificate from the
MITM CA; there is no passthrough tunnel.

A request read from a tunnel is for the `CONNECT` authority, while policy —
the filter, header rules, and the secret swap — judges its `Host`. So a
tunneled request whose `Host` or absolute URL names any other host is answered
`421` and audited as blocked, never sent: otherwise a credential bound to one
host could be sent to another. A tunnel whose client skips TLS is served in
plaintext; if the tunnel is to port 443, its requests still go upstream over
TLS (span attribute `proxy.http.tunnel_upgraded`). Zig's HTTP client
(ziglang/zig#19878) needs this: it sends plaintext HTTP inside an HTTPS
`CONNECT`. A tunnel to any other port stays plaintext end to end.

The sandbox-local bridge accepts localhost traffic from sandbox processes and
splices it, protocol-agnostic, onto an mTLS connection to the pool proxy
carrying the sandbox's client certificate. Its `Dialer` is how anything in a
sandbox reaches a pool service — the bridge, and the credentials relay in
`sandbox-agent/credentials` — and it has two layers:

- **Transport**, chosen by the URL's scheme through [`wire`](../wire), the same
  place every other transport in the system is chosen: `https://host:port`
  dials TCP (a Docker pool's `https://discobox-pool-proxy:17080`),
  `vsock://cid:port` an AF_VSOCK context, and `unix:///path` a socket, so a
  sandbox with no network interface at all can still reach its pool (ADR 0144
  §4). `http` is refused: nothing speaks plaintext to the pool.
- **mTLS**, identical on every transport. The client certificate's common name
  stays the tenant identity, so the proxy is unchanged and learns nothing about
  hypervisors. The pool's certificate is verified against `serverName` from
  `bridge.json`, or the URL's host when that is empty; a `vsock` or `unix` URL
  has no host, so it needs `serverName`, and the pool states it in every bridge
  config it stages.

The bridge lives in the dependency-light `proxy/bridge` subpackage so the
`sandbox-agent` binary (and `pool-agent/buildkitagent`'s per-build forwarder)
can embed it without pulling in the full pool proxy stack (goproxy, gormdb,
cache, audit). Pool-agent wiring
(`pool-agent/proxyagent`) runs the pool host proxy as a systemd unit, prepares
certificates, stages per-sandbox client material, and publishes sentinel sets
through `ApplyConfig`.

Client identity is the tenant boundary. Rules that can expose or restrict data
must support `ClientIDs`, and audit reads must support querying by client ID so
a caller can retrieve data for a specific sandbox without scanning or mixing
unrelated sandbox traffic.

## Certificate Model

Certificate preparation is independent of running the proxy:

- MITM CA: signs per-host certificates for intercepted HTTPS.
- mTLS CA: signs the pool host proxy server certificate and per-client
  certificates.
- Pool server certificate: presented by the pool host proxy listener.
- Client certificates: issued per sandbox/client identity (CN = client ID) and
  delivered in the sandbox's runtime-config document by pool-agent.

`PrepareCertificates` creates or reuses this material — reissuing anything within
`RenewBefore` of expiry, and the server certificate when it no longer covers
`ServerHosts` — and returns the `CertificateBundle` plus per-client
`ClientMaterial` (filesystem paths and proxy/CA environment values). Callers may
run it before the proxy process starts so certificates can be distributed during
sandbox setup.

### Renewal while a sandbox runs

A client certificate is renewed before it expires without restarting the
sandbox ([ADR 0126](../docs/adr/0126-a-sandbox-does-not-share-a-host-or-a-filesystem-with-its-pool.md)
§7):

- **The pool reissues** a client certificate within `RenewBefore` (30 days) of
  its expiry (365 days). Every status poll decides the sandbox's runtime-config
  document again, which calls `EnsureClientCertificate`, so a due certificate
  becomes a new revision the poll delivers
  ([pool-agent: Sandbox Runtime Config](../pool-agent/DESIGN.md#sandbox-runtime-config)).
- **The sandbox takes it without restarting.** `bridge.Material` reads the mTLS
  CA and keypair from their files on every handshake and re-parses them when
  their bytes change, so every holder of the key — the forwarders (egress,
  BuildKit, nested Docker), the credentials relay's `Dialer`, and the DNS stub —
  presents the renewed certificate from its next connection. A connection
  already open keeps the certificate it was opened with; it was valid when the
  pool verified it. The intake does not restart a bridge for material alone.
- **A half-delivered set keeps the last good one.** The intake replaces the
  certificate and key one at a time; a pair that does not load is ignored and
  tried again on the next handshake.
- **An expired certificate is never presented.** `Material.TLSConfig` refuses a
  certificate outside its validity before anything is dialed, so a sandbox the
  pool could not reach in time fails locally, saying it waits for the renewal,
  and recovers when it lands. A bridge may start on an expired certificate for
  the same reason: it serves once the renewal arrives.
- **The pool is still authenticated.** The CA that verifies the pool's server
  certificate is reloaded with the keypair, and verification is unchanged.
- **Only client certificates are renewed.** The pool's CAs and server
  certificate are issued for ten years, and CA rollover is not supported:
  `PrepareCertificates` would reissue an mTLS CA inside its last 30 days, but
  nothing re-signs the server or client certificates under it, and a running
  proxy keeps the CA it started with. Sandboxes would be delivered the new CA
  and refuse the running proxy's server certificate, and a restarted proxy would
  refuse every client certificate the old CA signed. A rollover needs the old
  and new CA trusted side by side while every leaf is re-signed; it is built
  before the first CA nears that window, not here.

The output registry needs no client authentication while it stays on the
Docker pool's private network: its unguessable repository names (ADR 0047)
are what protect it there. 0126 §7 requires authenticated pulls and deletions
only once a registry is reachable off that network; that is built with the
first backend that puts it there, not before.

## Persistence

Audit persistence uses `gormdb` with SQLite by default. The proxy package owns
schema migration and repository behavior. `gormdb` owns pool construction and
SQLite pragmas.

You're right that the time goes into delivering the git source. The cause is a full-history clone straight from GitHub, run inside the sandbox only after it has booted, and nothing reports progress while it runs. Thirty seconds into a slow clone, the status line switches to a message that is simply wrong.

## How a `-C owner/repo` source gets into the box

1. **Your machine:** the CLI expands the name to `https://github.com/discobox-ai/discobox.git` and runs a single `git ls-remote` to pin the commit (`cli/internal/sandboxcreate/source.go:733`, `:851`). That's fast, and the create call returns immediately with state `starting`.
2. **The pool** passes the GitHub URL itself to the sandbox as its origin. There is no pool-side mirror or cache (`pool-agent/sandboxruntime/sources.go:124`).
3. **The pool** builds and starts the container and waits for the sandbox agent to answer. Only then does it hand over the source list and start waiting for the clone (`runtime.go:686-698`).
4. **The sandbox agent** runs `git clone --no-checkout` with no `--depth` or `--filter`, through the pool's proxy (`sandbox-agent/sourceconverge/git.go:180`). The pool polls `/sources` every 500ms until it reports done.

## 1. Why it's slow

I measured it: I timed a real `discobox new -C discobox-ai/discobox -d` on station76 (box since archived), plus clones by hand.

| Step | Time |
|---|---|
| Create → sandbox agent ready for its sources | ~20s (container boot) |
| Clone | 9s in that run; 16s and 38s in two back-to-back runs in the same box; 13s to 7m13s from this machine |

- **It downloads the whole history.** That's 27.6 MiB and 35,477 objects, where a depth-1 clone is 7.5 MiB (~2.5s in the box) and a blobless clone is 3.5 MiB (~8s on this machine).
- **GitHub's speed swings a lot from run to run.** In the 38s clone, GitHub spent 14s compressing objects before sending anything, then sent at 765 KiB/s. In the 16s clone, compressing took 2s and the transfer ran at 2–7 MiB/s. Bigger downloads suffer more from this.
- **The clone waits for the container to boot.** It can't start until the sandbox agent is up, so boot time and clone time add together. A code comment says the pool used to clone before the container existed; ADR 0126 moved cloning into the sandbox.
- **Nothing is reused.** Every box clones from GitHub again. The proxy's response cache only stores registry `GET`s (`proxy/internal/cache/cache.go:528`), and git's fetch is a `POST`.
- **The proxy is not the bottleneck.** A 7 MB download through it ran at about host speed, with only 0.3–0.8s extra before the first byte. When conditions were good, the depth-1 clone inside the sandbox reached ~14 MiB/s.
- **No second container build.** The repo has no `.discobox/project.json`, so this path doesn't rebuild the container after the clone.

## 2. Why there's no useful feedback

- **The clone stage is announced once and never again.** The pool records `materializing_source` before it starts waiting and doesn't restate it while polling (`sources.go:404-454`).
- **The CLI ignores a phase older than 30 seconds** (`ProvisionProgressFresh`, `cli/internal/sandboxcreate/provisionstatus.go:34`, `:102`).
- **The fallback message is misleading.** While the clone runs, the box is still in state `pending`, because the pool's create call hasn't returned. So the status falls back to "waiting for the pool agent to become ready", then asks the pool, finds nothing recent, and keeps that line (`provisionstatus.go:68-75`, `:287`). For the first 30s you see "unpacking the source into the discobox"; after that it claims to be waiting for the pool agent, which has been ready the whole time.
- **No progress data exists to show anyway.** The agent's git output goes into a buffer that is only read on error, and git isn't asked for `--progress`. The `cloning` state carries no bytes, objects or URL.
- **The wording is wrong for this case.** "Unpacking the source" doesn't say the box is cloning from GitHub, which is what's actually happening.

Both the plain CLI and the console window build this line with the same function (`sandboxcreate.Status`), so both show the same thing.

## Ways to fix it (I haven't changed anything)
- Speed: clone shallow or blobless for remote-URL sources, keep a mirror on the pool to reuse, or start cloning while the container boots.
- Feedback: keep re-recording the phase while waiting, pass git's progress from the agent up through `/sources` into the status, and name the remote in the message.

content.text:
Running from `~/src/disco2` uses your machine as the git source: the CLI pushes the repo to station76, and the sandbox then clones it from the pool over your LAN. `-C discobox-ai/discobox` makes every box fetch the whole history from GitHub. I timed both on station76 (both test boxes since archived): **12s** from your checkout, versus 29s for the fastest `-C` run.

## Server picks one of three paths
The server decides how each source is delivered (`sourceNeedsPush`, `server/internal/resources/sandboxes/source_delivery.go:231`):

| Source | Delivery | Where the sandbox fetches from |
|---|---|---|
| Remote URL (`-C owner/repo`) | clone | GitHub, through the pool proxy |
| Local repo, server on the **same** machine | clone (bound) | The pool reads your `.git` directly |
| Local repo, server on **another** machine | push | A per-box empty repo on the pool, which your CLI pushes into |

Your primary server is station76 and your CLI runs in WSL, so you get the **push** path.

## How the push path works
1. **On your machine:** the CLI resolves HEAD (`886357d9`, `main`) and would snapshot uncommitted work (your tree was clean). It also reads `.discobox/sources.json` and finds sibling checkouts at `~/src/x` and `~/src/hooks`, so those two become local sources as well, not GitHub clones.
2. **Create:** the server marks all three sources `push`. The pool builds the box and parks it in `awaiting_source`.
3. **Push:** the CLI waits for that state ("waiting for the discobox to accept its source"), then runs `git push` for each source. The push goes to station76's git route, which forwards it to the pool's empty repo for that box (`cli/internal/sandboxcreate/deliver.go:89`, `server/internal/server/sandbox_git_proxy.go`). It pushes the full history of the pinned commit, which is about 23 MB for disco2. Then it calls `complete-source-push`.
4. **Clone:** the box resumes. The sandbox agent runs the same full `git clone`, but from the pool's own repo, so the data never leaves the LAN.

## Measured timeline (`discobox new -d`, from `~/src/disco2`)
| Time | Event |
|---|---|
| 15:55:09 | box created, container started |
| 15:55:10 | sandbox agent up (3 sources) |
| 15:55:16 | push of all 3 sources complete (~6s over the LAN) |
| 15:55:19 | primary cloned from the pool (~3s) |
| 15:55:20 | `hooks` and `x` cloned |
| 15:55:21 | ready |

The CLI returned after 8.8s.

## Comparison with `-C`
| | Local checkout (push) | `-C discobox-ai/discobox` |
|---|---|---|
| Who uploads the history | Your CLI, over the LAN to station76 | GitHub, to every box |
| History size | ~23 MB push + full clone from the pool | 27.6 MB full clone from GitHub |
| Speed limited by | LAN (steady, fast) | GitHub (compressing took 2–14s; transfer 0.7–7 MiB/s) |
| Extra sources from `sources.json` | Pushed from `~/src/x` and `~/src/hooks` | Not read: there's no local checkout to read it from |
| Can you see the slow part | Yes: "pushing source" comes from the CLI itself | Only "unpacking the source…" for 30s, then the wrong line |

Neither path is any smarter about git. Both clone the full history with no reuse between boxes. The local path is fast because the data comes over your LAN instead of from GitHub.

## Status messages differ too
- **Local:** the CLI does the slow step itself, so it can always say "pushing source". The clone afterwards takes about 3s, well inside the 30s window before a status goes stale, so the staleness bug never shows.
- **`-C`:** the slow step happens inside the sandbox and nothing reports it. Past 30s the line falls back to "waiting for the pool agent to become ready".

## Two other things I noticed (not investigated further)
- **Stale "waiting for Docker in the VM":** the local run showed this line even though the pool was long active and uses the Docker provider. The pool's own status seems to count as recent when it isn't. Same 30-second check, but on the pool record.
- **Boot time varied:** the sandbox agent took ~20s to come up in the `-C` run and 1s here. The source path doesn't explain that. It might have been a first boot on a freshly built image, but I didn't confirm it.

## What happens

`discobox new -C discobox-ai/discobox` (any remote-URL source) shows **"unpacking the source into the discobox"** for the first 30 seconds of the sandbox's clone. After that the line switches to **"waiting for the pool agent to become ready"**, which is wrong: the pool agent has been ready all along, and the sandbox is still cloning from GitHub. A clone of this repository from GitHub took anywhere from 9s to over a minute in testing, so the wrong line is often what users see for most of the wait.

Both the plain CLI and the console window build the line with `sandboxcreate.Status`, so both show it.

## Why

1. The pool agent publishes `materializing_source` **once**, just before `settleSources`, and never restates it while `awaitSourcesMaterialized` polls the sandbox every 500ms (`pool-agent/sandboxruntime/runtime.go:697`, `pool-agent/sandboxruntime/sources.go` `awaitSourcesMaterialized`).
2. The CLI ignores a recorded phase older than `ProvisionProgressFresh` (30s), on the premise that work in progress restates its phase continuously (`cli/internal/sandboxcreate/provisionstatus.go:34`, `recordedPhase`). Source materialization breaks that premise.
3. While the clone runs, the sandbox's `runtime.state` is still `pending`, because the pool's create call has not returned yet. So `ProvisionStatus` falls back to `StepWaitingForPool`. `Status` then asks the pool, finds no recent pool phase, and keeps "waiting for the pool agent to become ready" (`provisionstatus.go:68-75`, `Status`).

Observed on station76, sandbox `sbx_3xvkxkpes2tbtvr6`: `provisionProgress.phase=materializing_source` was stamped `15:42:25`. The sandbox agent logged `materialized source` at `15:42:33`. Nothing was published in between.

## Also missing

- **No progress to show.** The sandbox agent runs `git clone` without `--progress` and keeps its output in a buffer that is only read on error (`sandbox-agent/sourceconverge/git.go` `rawOutput`). `SourceState` carries only `cloning` and no bytes or object counts, so even a restated phase could not say how far the clone has got.
- **Wording.** "unpacking the source into the discobox" is wrong for a remote source. The sandbox is cloning `github.com/...`, and naming the remote would tell users where the time is going.

## Repro

```
discobox new -C discobox-ai/discobox
```

Watch the status line while the box comes up. If GitHub is fast that day and the clone finishes inside 30s, the bug won't show: try a larger repository, or throttle the network.

## Possible fixes (not prescriptive)

- Have the pool restate `materializing_source` on each `awaitSourcesMaterialized` poll, so it stays fresh for the whole clone.
- Better: pass the clone's progress (git `--progress` output, parsed into bytes and objects) from the sandbox agent's `/sources` route into the provision progress record, the way image pulls report `Pull`. Then render it, e.g. "cloning github.com/discobox-ai/discobox — 14.9 MiB, 50% objects".
- Name the source in the line.

Related write-up of timings and behavior on both delivery paths: see the companion issue.

Investigation of why `discobox new -C discobox-ai/discobox` feels slow, compared with `discobox new` run from a local checkout of the same repository. No code was changed. All measurements were taken on 2026-10-09 against a dev server on `station76` (Docker provider, default pool), from a WSL client on a different machine.

## Summary

- **A remote-URL source is a full-history clone from GitHub, made inside the sandbox after it boots.** Nothing is shared between boxes. Its cost is GitHub's speed at that moment, which varied from 9s to 7 minutes for the same 27.6 MiB.
- **A local checkout is push-delivered when the server is on another machine.** The CLI pushes the full history over the LAN to a per-box repository on the pool, and the sandbox clones from there. 12s end to end.
- **Neither path is smarter about git.** No shallow or partial clone, and no object reuse. The local path is faster only because the data travels over the LAN instead of from GitHub.
- The status line is wrong during long remote clones: see the companion bug issue.

## The three delivery paths

The server decides how each source is delivered (`sourceNeedsPush`, `server/internal/resources/sandboxes/source_delivery.go:231`):

| Source | Delivery | Where the sandbox fetches from |
|---|---|---|
| Remote URL (`-C owner/repo`) | clone | The remote itself (GitHub), through the pool proxy |
| Local repo, server on the same host | clone (bound) | The pool reads the developer's `.git` directly |
| Local repo, server on another host | push | A per-box empty repository on the pool, which the CLI pushes into |

## Remote-URL path (`-C discobox-ai/discobox`)

1. **Client:** expands the shorthand to `https://github.com/discobox-ai/discobox.git` and runs one `git ls-remote` to pin the commit (`cli/internal/sandboxcreate/source.go` `resolveRemoteRunSource`, `resolveRemoteGitRef`). The create call returns immediately with state `starting`.
2. **Pool:** passes the GitHub URL itself to the sandbox as its origin (`pool-agent/sandboxruntime/sources.go` `sourceOriginURL`). It builds and starts the container, waits for the sandbox agent, then calls `settleSources` and polls `/sources` until the clone is done.
3. **Sandbox agent:** runs `git clone --no-checkout [--branch X]` with no `--depth` or `--filter`, through the pool's proxy (`sandbox-agent/sourceconverge/git.go` `clone`).
4. **No reuse between boxes.** The proxy's response cache only admits registry `GET`s (`proxy/internal/cache/cache.go` `ShouldCache`), and git's fetch is a `POST`. The pool keeps no mirror.
5. **Declared sources are not read.** `.discobox/sources.json` is only read from a local checkout, so `x` and `hooks` do not arrive with a `-C` box.

### Timeline (sandbox `sbx_3xvkxkpes2tbtvr6`)

| Time (UTC) | Event |
|---|---|
| 15:42:04 | created; container started |
| 15:42:13 | pool's agent status poll still refused |
| 15:42:24 | sandbox agent: `wired sandbox sources count=1` (~20s of boot) |
| 15:42:25 | `materializing_source` recorded |
| 15:42:33 | `materialized source slug=primary`; ready |

So ~29s in total, of which ~9s was the clone, on a good network. The ~20s boot was much longer than in the local run below (1s). The source path doesn't explain that; it might be a first boot on a freshly built image, but that wasn't confirmed.

### How much the clone costs

Repository: 35,477 objects, 27.6 MiB pack, 25,762 deltas.

| Where | Kind | Time |
|---|---|---|
| WSL client → GitHub | full | 7m13s, 1m36s, 13s (three runs) |
| WSL client → GitHub | `--depth=1` | 3.1s (7.9 MiB) |
| WSL client → GitHub | `--filter=blob:none` | 8.1s (3.5 MiB) |
| station76 host → GitHub | full | 6s, 20s, 21s |
| Inside sandbox (via pool proxy) → GitHub | full | 16s, 30s, 38s, 47s |
| Inside sandbox (via pool proxy) → GitHub | `--depth=1` | 2.5s, 11s, 13s |

A breakdown of two back-to-back full clones in the same sandbox:

| Phase | Fast run | Slow run |
|---|---|---|
| GitHub: enumerating + counting | 0.9s | 0.9s |
| GitHub: compressing (server side) | 1.8s | 13.9s |
| Receiving 27.6 MiB | 12.8s (2–7 MiB/s) | 23.2s (765 KiB/s) |
| Resolving deltas | 0.2s | 0.3s |
| **Total** | **15.6s** | **38.3s** |

**The proxy is not the bottleneck.** A 7.1 MB codeload download through it reached 2.4–5.5 MB/s, against 4.4–6.3 MB/s directly from the station76 host, with 0.3–0.8s extra time-to-first-byte. A traced depth-1 clone inside the sandbox received 7.5 MiB at ~14 MiB/s. The variance is GitHub's (and the WAN's), and a full-history clone gives it the most room to hurt.

## Local-checkout path (`discobox new` in `~/src/disco2`, server on station76)

1. **Client:** resolves HEAD (`886357d9`, `main`) and the upstream URL, and would snapshot a dirty tree (`resolveLocalRunSource`). It reads `.discobox/sources.json` and finds sibling checkouts at `~/src/x` and `~/src/hooks`, so those become local sources too.
2. **Server:** client and server are on different hosts, so all three sources are marked `push`.
3. **Pool:** builds and starts the box and parks it in `awaiting_source`.
4. **Client:** waits for that state ("waiting for the discobox to accept its source"), then runs `git push` for each source. The push goes to the server's `git-origins` route, which forwards it to the pool's empty repository for that box (`cli/internal/sandboxcreate/deliver.go` `DeliverSource`/`pushSource`, `server/internal/server/sandbox_git_proxy.go`). It pushes the full history of the pinned commit, which is ~23 MB for disco2. Then it calls `complete-source-push`.
5. **Sandbox agent:** the same full `git clone`, from the pool-local origin through the proxy's origins host. No traffic leaves the LAN.

### Timeline (sandbox `sbx_ngfhsy3pzzndvxsy`)

| Time (UTC) | Event |
|---|---|
| 15:55:09 | created; container started |
| 15:55:10 | sandbox agent: `wired sandbox sources count=3` |
| 15:55:16 | push complete for all 3 sources (`sourceDeliveredAt`) |
| 15:55:19 | `materialized source slug=primary` |
| 15:55:20 | `hooks`, `x` materialized |
| 15:55:21 | ready |

12s in total; the CLI returned after 8.8s.

## Comparison

| | Local checkout (push) | `-C` remote URL |
|---|---|---|
| Who uploads the history | The CLI, over the LAN to the server | GitHub, to every box |
| Data moved | ~23 MB push + pool-local clone | 27.6 MiB clone over the WAN |
| Limited by | LAN | GitHub compression + WAN throughput |
| Declared sources (`sources.json`) | Delivered from sibling checkouts | Not delivered |
| Status during the slow step | "pushing source" (the client does it, so it knows) | 30s of "unpacking the source…", then a wrong line |
| Clone overlapped with boot | No | No |

## Ideas worth evaluating

- **Shallow or partial clone for remote-URL sources:** `--filter=blob:none` keeps the full history for `git log` and fetches blobs on demand; `--depth=1` is the smallest. This needs a decision about what a sandbox user expects from history.
- **A per-pool mirror or object cache for remote URLs**, so the second box from the same repository fetches only a delta. It could also apply to push-delivered origins, which today push the full history into an empty repository every time.
- **Start the remote clone while the container boots.** Before ADR 0126 the pool cloned before the container existed. Now cloning starts only after the sandbox agent answers.
- **Report clone progress** (see the companion bug issue).

## Smaller things noticed

- **Stale pool status:** during the local run, the CLI briefly showed "waiting for Docker in the VM" while the sandbox was `pending`, even though the pool had been `active` for a long time on the Docker provider. The pool's provision status apparently counts as recent when it isn't (`PoolProvisionStatus` applies the same 30s check). Not investigated further.
- **Boot time:** the sandbox agent took ~20s to come up in the remote run and 1s in the local run (see above).

I filed both issues in `discobox-ai/discobox`, and each one links to the other.

- **#138, the bug:** https://github.com/discobox-ai/discobox/issues/138. While a remote source is still cloning, the status line says "waiting for the pool agent to become ready".
  - **Cause:** the pool records "materializing source" only once, and the CLI ignores any status older than 30s. During the clone the box is still `pending`, so the line falls back to the pool-agent message.
  - **Also covers:** there's no clone progress to show, and the "unpacking the source" wording is wrong for a GitHub clone.
  - It includes repro steps and fix options, and is labelled `bug`, `area/cli`, `area/pool-agent` and `area/sandbox-agent`.
- **#139, the timing write-up:** https://github.com/discobox-ai/discobox/issues/139. It compares the three ways a source gets into a box and walks through the `-C` path and the push path step by step. It also covers:
  - both measured timelines (29s with `-C`, 12s from your checkout) and the clone measurements: full, depth-1 and blobless, from this machine, the station76 host and inside the box;
  - why the pool proxy isn't the bottleneck;
  - the speed-up ideas: shallow or blobless clones, a per-pool mirror, and starting the clone while the container boots;
  - the two side observations: the stale "waiting for Docker in the VM" line and the 20s vs 1s boot.

  It's labelled `enhancement`, `area/pool-agent`, `area/sandbox-agent` and `area/cli`.

I didn't add priority or `triaged` labels, so triage can set those.
